content.text: Full-stack with .NET and Angular isn't two frameworks learned side by side; it's owning a feature from the database table to the screen. This roadmap gets you there in eight stages, with one project that grows through all of them.

Two weeks into her first full-stack job, a new developer gets a ticket: "The orders page takes eight seconds and sometimes shows yesterday's totals." She finished a .NET course and an Angular course, and both halves look like the examples she studied. The bug lives between them: the component calls the API once per row, each call runs an EF Core query on a column with no index, and a cache header keeps the old totals on screen. Neither course covered that gap.
The belief: full-stack means two frameworks. Learn ASP.NET Core for the server and Angular for the browser, and you're a full-stack developer.
It's a fair reading of the market. Job ads list frameworks, courses sell one at a time, and both carry a lot for you: ASP.NET Core ships
, configuration and authentication, and Angular ships a router, forms and a CLI. You do need both.

But the frameworks are the two ends, and the work is in the middle: the HTTP contract, the SQL the ORM writes, who may see which row, and how both halves get deployed. Microsoft's own EF Core overview calls intermediate knowledge of the database server essential for production apps. The framework assumes that knowledge; it doesn't replace it.
You own features from the table to the screen. A feature like "customers can save a delivery address" touches every layer:

items.text: The table, its constraints and the EF Core migration, plus the SQL it produces.
The endpoint: validation, authorization (only the owner may edit) and an error the client can show.
The Angular form and the service that calls the API, with loading and error states.
Tests on both sides, and at least one that goes through both.
The pipeline, per-environment configuration and the logs that tell you when something breaks.

content.text: Around that: code review, reading the network tab next to the server logs, and agreeing with product people on what "done" means.
The stages from zero to senior

The ranges assume about 10 hours a week; more hours shorten them. Grow one project through every stage instead of starting a new tutorial each time. The roadmap targets .NET 10, the LTS release supported until November 2028, and Angular 22. .NET 11 shipped in November 2026 as a two-year STS release, and Angular now ships one major version a year, so these skills carry over.

Books explain the reasons behind the APIs; the docs track the current API. Use both:

rows.text: C# 14 and .NET 10 – Modern Cross-Platform Development Fundamentals

content.text: Three of these books are older than this roadmap's versions. ASP.NET Core in Action covers .NET 7 and Entity Framework Core in Action covers EF Core 5: their chapters on the pipeline, dependency injection, auth, change tracking and performance still hold, but check newer APIs on Microsoft Learn. Learning Angular covers Angular 19, three major versions behind: read it for the concepts and check every API on angular.dev.

items.text: You can't tell which half a bug lives in. Finish the API stages first.
Skipping SQL because EF Core exists.
The ORM writes the SQL; it doesn't read the execution plan for you.
Ten tutorial apps instead of one real one.
Tutorials skip what hurts: auth, errors, deployment and changing a schema that holds data.
An enterprise template for a small app.
Four projects and a repository per table make a CRUD app harder to change, not cleaner.
The first deploy then exposes problems you designed in months earlier.

content.text: Keep one browser tab on the network panel and one terminal on the API logs. Most full-stack bugs are a mismatch between the request the browser sent and the one the server thinks it received.

Don't build your own login or password hashing. ASP.NET Core ships authentication, authorization and data protection: use them, or a trusted identity provider, and spend your time on the authorization rules, which only you can write for your app.
Nobody who hires you can see your courses; they can see your project. One finished thing beats many half-done ones:

items.text: A live URL and a public repository whose README says what the app does and how to run it with one command.
Tests that run in CI, with the pipeline history visible.
A short write-up of one hard bug, such as an N+1 query you fixed, with before and after numbers you measured.
A clean history of small commits with clear messages.

Full-stack means owning a feature from the table to the screen; HTTP, SQL, auth and deployment are the middle the frameworks leave to you.
Learn in order: C#, the API, SQL with EF Core, auth, the web platform and TypeScript, Angular, then testing and deployment.
Grow one project through every stage and finish it; that project is your portfolio.
Target .NET 10 LTS and Angular 22: books for the concepts, Microsoft Learn and angular.dev for the current APIs.
